Gill Nets: Plundering our Dams and Rivers

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Unabated poaching in our rivers and dams is threatening our freshwater biodiversity...

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa has comprehensive environmental legislation but when it comes to enforcing the law we fall short. Our freshwater fish and aquatic biodiversity in our rivers and dams are being decimated by relentless gill net poaching and even though it is illegal to even own a gill net, you find hundreds of kilometers of nets in our provincial dams and rivers. The nets are not selective and every fish in the river will end up in the net, and often other biodiversity will also become intangled in the nets. Foreigners are mostly blamed for the practice, coming in from neighbouring countries and seeing our freshwater systems as easy pickings. Nets are even regularly reported in the Vaal river, Orange river up to Richtersveld, and as far as the Crocodile River and the Zambezi -- The problem is far-reaching

Summary:
Belinda Joubert lives on the banks of the Crocodile river in Broederstroom. For the past 5 years she has witnessed gill nets in the river on a daily basis. The nets are deployed in the evening and then taken out in the early morning. The fish, she says, are sold at a nearby market on the side of a busy road. Of particular concern is the large number of by-catch. She has photos of lizards and various birds being entangled int he nets -- even a kudu. But this is not an isolated incident. Many of our rivers and dams are being plundered in this way. Just this week a 3km net was taken out at a dam just outside Rust de Winter and dams like Renosterkop, on the border between Gauteng and Mpumalanga are riddled with gill nets on a daily basis. The NGO Eco-Care Trust, reports that sometimes large trucks are seen on the edges of dams, ready to take the fish away. By catch, or fish that are too injured for consumption are simply left to rot in the rams and rivers. The Eco-Care Trust was established in 1995 to conserve our freshwater aquatic ecosystems. They have a vast network of volunteers that keep an eye on our rivers and dams and report and remove illegal nets. Eco-Care Trust will take us to a dam and show us the illegal nets and we will be part of the operation to remove the illegal nets.

New legislation tabled for comment will potentially make all this gillnetting legal, which could have dire consequences for our freshwater biodiversity. The Government wants to make "traditional" fishing legal, giving indigent communities access to a valuable source of food, but without the necessary management and policing this could end up being disastrous. A pilot project in conjunction with Rhodes University in the VanderKloof dam in the Northern Cape wanted to pave the way for small scale commercial fishing operations, but the effect on the endangered largemouth yellowfish was devastating and the project was halted after much resistance from the conservation and angling community.

Further information:
Unlawful gill nets are a large problem in South African dams and rivers. Eco-Care Trust receives reports of gill nets in several areas of South Africa on a weekly basis. The problem is not the utilisation of the fish resource, but the uncontrolled whipping out of fish populations in our dams and rivers. You can only utilise a resource if the resource has the capacity in terms of size and right fish species diversity. Unfortunately gill nets are very much a non-selective method of utilisation and fish caught in the nets are doomed to death because of the injuries sustained in the nets. Therefore, if there are protected fish species in the aquatic system, gillnetting may totally destroy that fish species in that system. Furthermore, if permits to net fish are to be issued, the policing of the permits are absolutely essential. Sustainable utilisation is the requirements for biodiversity. Taking all these factors into consideration, sustainable fishing by subsistence anglers and sport anglers, instead of commercial netting, appears to be the solution to support the economy and provide for the needy. This statement is backed by well-founded research.

The Inland Fishing Policy has been tabled for public comment and will be gazetted in the near future. this is worrying since it will legalise "traditional" fishing, which will open the doors to uncontrolled gillnetting even more. The government's stance is that our rivers and dams are a source of food for indigent communities, but gill nets are about making money, and not simply feeding a family. Eco-Care Trust says syndicates are involved in the large-scale netting in some of our dams -- often in the middle of nature reserves, and there is very little policing or political will to curb this.

Gillnetting in rivers is of particular concern because it has the potential to wipe out indigenous and endangered yellowfish. In dams, Blue Kurpers are targeted, but of course, the nets are indescriminent and everything is taken out, irrespective of the season... often a whole generation of fish is wiped out as the pregnant females are caught. Our rivers and dams can simply not sustain this onslaught.

ROUGH TREATMENT:
We begin on a Boat on the Klipvoordam in the Borakalalo National Park in NorthWest Province... Taking out nets. Claire helping to cut fish loose. Eco-Care Trust Volunteers talk about their experiences, how many nets they have seen and taken out in various dams and rivers. It is an isolated spot, away from the public eye so it's easy for the people to fish unnoticed... Speak to Bernard Venter (angler and Eco-Care Trust Secretary)... But the fishermen are brazen, even netting in the Crocodile River in Broederstroom... We speak to Belinda Joubert -- gill netting on her doorstep... decimation of wildlife, no assistance from authorities. ... New legislation will make all this legal. Speak to Department of Environment & Fisheries -- is this a good idea? Talk about govt pilot project in the Northern Cape that has been halted because of the impact on largemouth yellowfish. Speak to netting expert Leon Barkhuizen and Andre Hoffman of Mpumalanga Parks and Tourism who are against the netting. Mention that netting is traditional way of fishing in Malawi and Caprivi, but not in SA... There it was sustainable to some extent because nets were hand-made. Now the nets are longer and easily obtained and fairly cheap -- some fishermen are even using netting used in the packaging and transport of vegetables, and shade netting. Speak to Capt johan Grobler of Mpumalanga SAPS about the difficulties they have in prosecuting illegal fishermen. Lack of support from Nature Conservation. Speak to Govt about the way forward... can the tide be turned?

Press Release:


Gill Net Poaching
Dams across the country are fast running out of freshwater fish – the culprit – indiscriminate fishing with gill nets. It’s illegal in South Africa to fish using these nets but that hasn’t stopped poachers from throwing hundreds of metres of these nets across large water bodies, catching everything in their wake. The environmental legislation against this practice is clear, but when it comes to enforcing the law, authorities fall short. Carte Blanche heads out on the water to investigate this trend.
Producer: Stenette Grosskopf
Presenter: Claire Mawisa
Watch the trailer


Script:


Illegal Gill Nets


V/O
The Klipvoordam in the Borakalalo National Park lies about 60 kms north of Brits in the North West Province. The 800ha dam was established in 1970 and despite the heavy pollution load from upsteam Gauteng users, a large pod of hippos call it home. But although it looks peaceful on the surface... a line of polystyrene floaters reveals the truth...

In these waters lurk hundreds of metres of illegal gillnets...
UPSOUND BERNARD
I'm going to cut it here and we work back...
V/O
Bernard Venter runs Eco-Care Trust, and together with a team of volunteers and Park Rangers they've taken us out on the dam to show the extent of the gillnet problem...
Bernard Venter
Eco-care trust is an NGO. We’re working in the field of water conservation and especially aquatic monitoring and this is one of the projects that we’re running is taking out gillnets, illegal gillnets.
V/O
The first net they pull out if filled with Mozambique Tillapia, or Blue Kurper as they are commonly known – an indigenous freshwater fish that is becoming scarcer.
UPSOUND BERNARD
In the past we've had blue Kurpers of 2/3 kgs but we don't find those size of kurpers anymore in the dam.
V/O
A gillnet is crafted from fishing line and is submerged in the water like a long curtain, weighted at the bottom by small rocks. At the top end they use polystyrene cubes and half-filled 2l plastic bottles...
Bernard Venter
Claire: Just explain to somebody who doesn’t understand why gillnets are illegal. What does the gillnet actually do to the fish or the… the animal that it catches?

Bernard: Very often, the gillnet is catching the fish in the gills, so that it’s causing damage to the gills and also the protective layer around the fish, it’s get damage, and the scales are getting damaged, then the fish gets fungi infections.
V/O
Gillnets are indiscriminate, meaning that you catch all species of fish in the dam or river, even the ones you are supposed to conserve. And very often other animals become entangled in the nets.
UPSOUND BERNARD
We often find terrapins in the nets as well as birds.
V/O
Venter decides to drag this gillnet to the edge of the water where the park rangers are ready to cut the entangled fish loose...
CLAIRE
So unfortunately even though the net is out of the water it was too late for these little fishies... No but he's alive... must I put him back?

I hope so...

Unfortunately the fish didn't make it, as you can see.. They're moving but they're floating.
V/o
Along the edge of the dam there is evidence that the poachers are not very far away..

The fire is still smouldering... and hidden under the grass is some of this morning's pickings.
UPSOUND
Moses: Some of them are still alive

Bernard: Yes, I can see.
Bernard Venter:
Claire: So you say they just hide their boats and canoes?

Ja, they hide it underneath the surface, the canoes. Put stones in the canoes and sink it underneath the surface, you can see it's very dirty the water so you can't see it it's under the water. This they covered it so you can't recognise it easily.
V/O
With the aid of makeshift garden-rake-oars, the poachers skillfully navigate the dam and set their gillnets night after night.
LINK
This morning I spent 1 hour on 1 dam and we managed to pull out hundreds of metres of illegal gill nets. Now imagine, there are hundreds of dams in South Africa, and a vast river network... So we're talking about a huge amount of fish that are poached every single day.
V/O
Country-wide we simply do not have the resources to fight this type of onslaught.
Johnson
The wildlife security unit looks after game, they look after tourists, they after this. So, there’s not enough, we’ve only got twenty-three rangers that have to deal with all this...
V/O
North West Parks Board regional manager Johnson Maoka admits that more needs to be done to curb the relentless poaching...
Johnson
There’s a community awareness program which is, you know, spread out through the communities to say to people to not poach, to not catch fish illegally, but these people have established businesses out of this illegal fishing. Therefore, it is difficult for them to just stop overnight.
V/O

Whilst many fish to put food on the table, it seems fishing with gillnets is driven by greed.
Johnson
The gangs have grown, just, out of hand. There’re more than ten gangs coming in at different places every night. They carry all sorts of weapons. They’ve been found to be carrying guns, they’ve been found to be carrying knives, et cetera.
V/O
And it seems to be pretty much the same story at most of our dams...
Whatsapp video – Rust de Winter

Roodekoppies
Illegally fishing with gillnets is also happening in most of our rivers, even here in the Crocodile river just before the inlet into Hartbeespoort Dam.
Belinda Joubert
They don’t just take one fish out they there… there’s like hundreds and I mean you know those big bags that you get? … We counted the bags like between four and six bags a day and then you have six or seven people doing that so you can imagine for yourself what amount of fish they take...

For the past 3 years Belinda Joubert has been waging war against the poachers and regularly removes the nets on her doorstep. She's concerned about the greater eco-system of the area.
Belinda Joubert
We had hundreds of flamingos, we had hundreds of cormorants, the likkewane, the Egyptian geese, so by doing that they actually just take out the whole system – there's nothing left.
V/O
We approached the fishermen at the opposite side of the riverbank but most were reluctant to speak to us.

00:37:54:18 - 00:38:02:09
Claire: are there any people fishing with fishing nets?
fisherman: i don’t know about other places and people but here we use rods
V/O
Although he insists they use rods, there are piles of fish scales and polystyrene bits all over the veld.

00:38:02:06 - 00:38:19:19
Claire: what is the reason for you guys fishing on this dam?
Fisherman: what are we suppose to do when we need money. Fishing is a
way for us to make money. We sell the fish and that's how we make
money.
LINK
In developing regions and countries freshwater fish is the staple diet for many communities but in South Africa we have wide-spread access to other sources of protein so fish from our river and dams is often overlooked.
V/O
But freshwater fish is relatively cheap and is becoming more and more sought after in the poorer communities.
Casper Kruger
The demand is much bigger than you all know. If they’re catching fish like tonight, they’re selling all over. In Hartbeespoort dam average, maybe two, three tonnes a night.
V/O
Casper Kruger owns one of SA's very few licensed commercial freshwater fisheries and is passionate about the industry.

UPSOUND CAS


Kruger says with proper controls and training it can all be turned around into a profitable country-wide industry.
Casper Kruger
It’s a good thing to harvest fish from any lake on a regular base, so you get the old ones out, the overstock of fish out of the system, the other fish will get stronger and breed more. It is a good thing to do it in a right way.

Claire: Hm, but not the way they’re doing it now.

No, now you catch any fish.
LINK
The National Department of Environment, which now includes Forestry and Fisheries declined an on-camera interview, but sent us a written response – which basically states that they are aware of the problem of illegal gill netting and that they believe the new National Freshwater Wild Capture Fisheries Policy is the answer.
V/O
The Department states that it discourages breaking the law. The new policy framework which is currently up for public comment is the first step towards the sustainable growth of the sector and will include legislative reform, definition of access rights and the empowerment of rural communities.
Prof Hara
The National Fisheries Policy Framework which is currently being developed is supposed to regularise the sector and and also try and effectively develop rules and regulations about use of the sector.. sustainably.
V/O
Prof Mafaniso Hara from the Institute for Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies at UWC believes that our dams can be used more effectively, but stresses that increased use must be accompanied by strong management policies.
Prof Hara
What we have is a situation by where the resources in dams is supposed to be natural, we should use it in such a way that it can reproduce and renew itself without restocking.
Bernard Venter
A dam is like a game reserve. When you drive through a game reserve, you can see what is in the game reserve, but you can’t see is underneath the surface of the dam. So, you need to keep that balance and see what is inside and know what is inside and what you can take out and how much of that...
V/O
These gillnets will never be used for illegal fishing again, but unfortunately it seems that tomorrow there'll be fresh ones ready to catch what is left in our dams and rivers....
Bernard Venter
You need rangers to look after our dams. South Africa, we don’t have dedicated rangers. Knowing enough about the problem and knowing enough about the dam.


TEASER 1 11”
Thousands of metres of illegal gill nets lurk in the waters of our public dams and rivers. Will the indiscriminate poaching be stopped in time to save our freshwater fish?


TEASER 2 11”
Large-scale illegal gillnetting is commonplace in our dams and rivers and the poaching is escalating... Could new legislation giving increased fishing rights to communities be the answer?


TEASER 3 11”
Armed gangs poach tonnes of fish from our dams and rivers with illegal gill nets. How do we safeguard our aquatic biodiversity and still give people access to this valuable foodsource?

Bernard: Very often, the gillnet is catching the fish in the gills, so that it’s causing damage to the gills and also the protective layer around the fish, it’s get damage, and the scales are getting damaged, then the fish gets fungi infections. V/O Gillnets are indiscriminate, meaning that you catch all species of fish in the dam or river, even the ones you are supposed to conserve. And very often other animals become entangled in the nets. UPSOUND BERNARD We often find terrapins in the nets as well as birds. V/O Venter decides to drag this gillnet to the edge of the water where the park rangers are ready to cut the entangled fish loose... CLAIRE So unfortunately even though the net is out of the water it was too late for these little fishies... No but he's alive... must I put him back? I hope so... Unfortunately the fish didn't make it, as you can see.. They're moving but they're floating. V/o Along the edge of the dam there is evidence that the poachers are not very far away.. The fire is still smouldering... and hidden under the grass is some of this morning's pickings. UPSOUND Moses: Some of them are still alive Bernard: Yes, I can see. Bernard Venter: Claire: So you say they just hide their boats and canoes? Ja, they hide it underneath the surface, the canoes. Put stones in the canoes and sink it underneath the surface, you can see it's very dirty the water so you can't see it it's under the water. This they covered it so you can't recognise it easily. V/O With the aid of makeshift garden-rake-oars, the poachers skillfully navigate the dam and set their gillnets night after night. LINK This morning I spent 1 hour on 1 dam and we managed to pull out hundreds of metres of illegal gill nets. Now imagine, there are hundreds of dams in South Africa, and a vast river network... So we're talking about a huge amount of fish that are poached every single day. V/O Country-wide we simply do not have the resources to fight this type of onslaught. Johnson The wildlife security unit looks after game, they look after tourists, they after this. So, there’s not enough, we’ve only got twenty-three rangers that have to deal with all this... V/O North West Parks Board regional manager Johnson Maoka admits that more needs to be done to curb the relentless poaching... Johnson There’s a community awareness program which is, you know, spread out through the communities to say to people to not poach, to not catch fish illegally, but these people have established businesses out of this illegal fishing. Therefore, it is difficult for them to just stop overnight. V/O Whilst many fish to put food on the table, it seems fishing with gillnets is driven by greed. Johnson The gangs have grown, just, out of hand. There’re more than ten gangs coming in at different places every night. They carry all sorts of weapons. They’ve been found to be carrying guns, they’ve been found to be carrying knives, et cetera. V/O And it seems to be pretty much the same story at most of our dams... Whatsapp video – Rust de Winter Roodekoppies Illegally fishing with gillnets is also happening in most of our rivers, even here in the Crocodile river just before the inlet into Hartbeespoort Dam. Belinda Joubert They don’t just take one fish out they there… there’s like hundreds and I mean you know those big bags that you get? … We counted the bags like between four and six bags a day and then you have six or seven people doing that so you can imagine for yourself what amount of fish they take... For the past 3 years Belinda Joubert has been waging war against the poachers and regularly removes the nets on her doorstep. She's concerned about the greater eco-system of the area. Belinda Joubert We had hundreds of flamingos, we had hundreds of cormorants, the likkewane, the Egyptian geese, so by doing that they actually just take out the whole system – there's nothing left. V/O We approached the fishermen at the opposite side of the riverbank but most were reluctant to speak to us. 00:37:54:18 - 00:38:02:09 Claire: are there any people fishing with fishing nets? fisherman: i don’t know about other places and people but here we use rods V/O Although he insists they use rods, there are piles of fish scales and polystyrene bits all over the veld. 00:38:02:06 - 00:38:19:19 Claire: what is the reason for you guys fishing on this dam? Fisherman: what are we suppose to do when we need money. Fishing is a way for us to make money. We sell the fish and that's how we make money. LINK In developing regions and countries freshwater fish is the staple diet for many communities but in South Africa we have wide-spread access to other sources of protein so fish from our river and dams is often overlooked. V/O But freshwater fish is relatively cheap and is becoming more and more sought after in the poorer communities. Casper Kruger The demand is much bigger than you all know. If they’re catching fish like tonight, they’re selling all over. In Hartbeespoort dam average, maybe two, three tonnes a night. V/O Casper Kruger owns one of SA's very few licensed commercial freshwater fisheries and is passionate about the industry. UPSOUND CAS Kruger says with proper controls and training it can all be turned around into a profitable country-wide industry. Casper Kruger It’s a good thing to harvest fish from any lake on a regular base, so you get the old ones out, the overstock of fish out of the system, the other fish will get stronger and breed more. It is a good thing to do it in a right way. Claire: Hm, but not the way they’re doing it now. No, now you catch any fish. LINK The National Department of Environment, which now includes Forestry and Fisheries declined an on-camera interview, but sent us a written response – which basically states that they are aware of the problem of illegal gill netting and that they believe the new National Freshwater Wild Capture Fisheries Policy is the answer. V/O The Department states that it discourages breaking the law. The new policy framework which is currently up for public comment is the first step towards the sustainable growth of the sector and will include legislative reform, definition of access rights and the empowerment of rural communities. Prof Hara The National Fisheries Policy Framework which is currently being developed is supposed to regularise the sector and and also try and effectively develop rules and regulations about use of the sector.. sustainably. V/O Prof Mafaniso Hara from the Institute for Poverty, Land and Agrarian Studies at UWC believes that our dams can be used more effectively, but stresses that increased use must be accompanied by strong management policies. Prof Hara What we have is a situation by where the resources in dams is supposed to be natural, we should use it in such a way that it can reproduce and renew itself without restocking. Bernard Venter A dam is like a game reserve. When you drive through a game reserve, you can see what is in the game reserve, but you can’t see is underneath the surface of the dam. So, you need to keep that balance and see what is inside and know what is inside and what you can take out and how much of that... V/O These gillnets will never be used for illegal fishing again, but unfortunately it seems that tomorrow there'll be fresh ones ready to catch what is left in our dams and rivers.... Bernard Venter You need rangers to look after our dams. South Africa, we don’t have dedicated rangers. Knowing enough about the problem and knowing enough about the dam. TEASER 1 11” Thousands of metres of illegal gill nets lurk in the waters of our public dams and rivers. Will the indiscriminate poaching be stopped in time to save our freshwater fish? TEASER 2 11” Large-scale illegal gillnetting is commonplace in our dams and rivers and the poaching is escalating... Could new legislation giving increased fishing rights to communities be the answer? TEASER 3 11” Armed gangs poach tonnes of fish from our dams and rivers with illegal gill nets. How do we safeguard our aquatic biodiversity and still give people access to this valuable foodsource?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Unabated poaching in our rivers and dams is threatening our freshwater biodiversity...
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa has comprehensive environmental legislation but when it comes to enforcing the law we fall short. Our freshwater fish and aquatic biodiversity in our rivers and dams are being decimated by relentless gill net poaching and even though it is illegal to even own a gill net, you find hundreds of kilometers of nets in our provincial dams and rivers. The nets are not selective and every fish in the river will end up in the net, and often other biodiversity will also become intangled in the nets. Foreigners are mostly blamed for the practice, coming in from neighbouring countries and seeing our freshwater systems as easy pickings. Nets are even regularly reported in the Vaal river, Orange river up to Richtersveld, and as far as the Crocodile River and the Zambezi -- The problem is far-reaching
metadata.Summary: Belinda Joubert lives on the banks of the Crocodile river in Broederstroom. For the past 5 years she has witnessed gill nets in the river on a daily basis. The nets are deployed in the evening and then taken out in the early morning. The fish, she says, are sold at a nearby market on the side of a busy road. Of particular concern is the large number of by-catch. She has photos of lizards and various birds being entangled int he nets -- even a kudu. But this is not an isolated incident. Many of our rivers and dams are being plundered in this way. Just this week a 3km net was taken out at a dam just outside Rust de Winter and dams like Renosterkop, on the border between Gauteng and Mpumalanga are riddled with gill nets on a daily basis. The NGO Eco-Care Trust, reports that sometimes large trucks are seen on the edges of dams, ready to take the fish away. By catch, or fish that are too injured for consumption are simply left to rot in the rams and rivers. The Eco-Care Trust was established in 1995 to conserve our freshwater aquatic ecosystems. They have a vast network of volunteers that keep an eye on our rivers and dams and report and remove illegal nets. Eco-Care Trust will take us to a dam and show us the illegal nets and we will be part of the operation to remove the illegal nets. New legislation tabled for comment will potentially make all this gillnetting legal, which could have dire consequences for our freshwater biodiversity. The Government wants to make "traditional" fishing legal, giving indigent communities access to a valuable source of food, but without the necessary management and policing this could end up being disastrous. A pilot project in conjunction with Rhodes University in the VanderKloof dam in the Northern Cape wanted to pave the way for small scale commercial fishing operations, but the effect on the endangered largemouth yellowfish was devastating and the project was halted after much resistance from the conservation and angling community.
metadata.Further information: Unlawful gill nets are a large problem in South African dams and rivers. Eco-Care Trust receives reports of gill nets in several areas of South Africa on a weekly basis. The problem is not the utilisation of the fish resource, but the uncontrolled whipping out of fish populations in our dams and rivers. You can only utilise a resource if the resource has the capacity in terms of size and right fish species diversity. Unfortunately gill nets are very much a non-selective method of utilisation and fish caught in the nets are doomed to death because of the injuries sustained in the nets. Therefore, if there are protected fish species in the aquatic system, gillnetting may totally destroy that fish species in that system. Furthermore, if permits to net fish are to be issued, the policing of the permits are absolutely essential. Sustainable utilisation is the requirements for biodiversity. Taking all these factors into consideration, sustainable fishing by subsistence anglers and sport anglers, instead of commercial netting, appears to be the solution to support the economy and provide for the needy. This statement is backed by well-founded research. The Inland Fishing Policy has been tabled for public comment and will be gazetted in the near future. this is worrying since it will legalise "traditional" fishing, which will open the doors to uncontrolled gillnetting even more. The government's stance is that our rivers and dams are a source of food for indigent communities, but gill nets are about making money, and not simply feeding a family. Eco-Care Trust says syndicates are involved in the large-scale netting in some of our dams -- often in the middle of nature reserves, and there is very little policing or political will to curb this. Gillnetting in rivers is of particular concern because it has the potential to wipe out indigenous and endangered yellowfish. In dams, Blue Kurpers are targeted, but of course, the nets are indescriminent and everything is taken out, irrespective of the season... often a whole generation of fish is wiped out as the pregnant females are caught. Our rivers and dams can simply not sustain this onslaught. ROUGH TREATMENT: We begin on a Boat on the Klipvoordam in the Borakalalo National Park in NorthWest Province... Taking out nets. Claire helping to cut fish loose. Eco-Care Trust Volunteers talk about their experiences, how many nets they have seen and taken out in various dams and rivers. It is an isolated spot, away from the public eye so it's easy for the people to fish unnoticed... Speak to Bernard Venter (angler and Eco-Care Trust Secretary)... But the fishermen are brazen, even netting in the Crocodile River in Broederstroom... We speak to Belinda Joubert -- gill netting on her doorstep... decimation of wildlife, no assistance from authorities. ... New legislation will make all this legal. Speak to Department of Environment & Fisheries -- is this a good idea? Talk about govt pilot project in the Northern Cape that has been halted because of the impact on largemouth yellowfish. Speak to netting expert Leon Barkhuizen and Andre Hoffman of Mpumalanga Parks and Tourism who are against the netting. Mention that netting is traditional way of fishing in Malawi and Caprivi, but not in SA... There it was sustainable to some extent because nets were hand-made. Now the nets are longer and easily obtained and fairly cheap -- some fishermen are even using netting used in the packaging and transport of vegetables, and shade netting. Speak to Capt johan Grobler of Mpumalanga SAPS about the difficulties they have in prosecuting illegal fishermen. Lack of support from Nature Conservation. Speak to Govt about the way forward... can the tide be turned?
